label: L12
title: Kernel methods for data-driven optimization
brief: Lecture 12 solves the conditional stochastic problem $\min_{z\in Z}\mathbb E[c(z;y)\mid x=x_0]$ from data $(x_i,y_i)$ by kernel regression (Bertsimas and Koduri). It starts from the Bertsimas–Kallus weighted-SAA idea and linear regression, then generalizes to nonlinear predictions with reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and the Representer Theorem. Two routes follow: kerobj predicts the objective $h(z,x)\approx\mathbb E[c(z;y)|x]$ in closed form and minimizes it over $z$; keropt learns the decision rule $\hat z(x)=\sum_i a_iK(x_i,x)$ directly through a finite-dimensional problem in $a$. Each comes with a convergence theorem, and keropt is convex with $nd$ variables when $c$ is convex. Expect questions on the RKHS / kernel definitions, the Representer Theorem, the two formulations and their closed forms, the convergence conditions, constraint handling, and the newsvendor comparison.
kp: Bertsimas–Kallus: local ML gives $\mathbb E[y|x_0]\approx\sum_i w(x_i,x_0)y_i$, so solve $\min_z\sum_i w(x_i,x_0)c(z;y_i)$.
Linear regression version: $\min_z c(z;Y)^Tw$ with $w=X(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$; kernels make it nonlinear.
PD kernel: every Gram matrix $[K(\bar x^i,\bar x^j)]$ is PSD; the RKHS is the closure of $\{\sum_i\bar a_iK(\bar x_i,\cdot)\}$.
Kernels: linear $x^Tx'$ (linear functions), polynomial $(x^Tx'+r)^d$ (degree $\le d$), Gaussian $\exp(-\|x-x'\|^2/2\sigma^2)$ (approximates any continuous bounded function).
Representer Theorem: $\min_{f\in H}\sum_iV(f(x_i);y_i)+\lambda\|f\|_H$ has a solution $f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^na_iK(x_i,x)$.
kerobj: $h(z,x)=K(X,x)^T(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}c(z;Y)$, then $\min_{z\in Z}h(z,x_0)$; square loss because the conditional mean minimizes MSE.
keropt: $\hat z(x)=\sum_ia_iK(x_i,x)$ with $a=\arg\min_a\frac1n\sum_ic((\hat Ka)_i;y_i)+\lambda a^T\hat Ka$; for $z\in\mathbb R^d$ use $d$ coefficient vectors.
Constraints: penalty $\psi\sum_j\max(f_j(z),0)^2$ with $\psi\to\infty$, then project $\min_{z\in Z}\|z-\hat z(x_0)\|^2$ if needed. Convex $c$ ⇒ convex problem in $nd$ variables.
keropt converges if $c$ is Lipschitz and convex, $\sup K(x,x)\le\kappa^2$, $c(0;y)\le C_0$, $K$ universal, $\lambda\to0$ and $\lambda\sqrt n\to\infty$.

topics.x: We want $\min_{z\in Z}\mathbb E[c(z;y)|x=x_0]$ from data. Local methods (Bertsimas–Kallus) and linear regression both express the conditional cost as a weighted sum of sample costs $c(z;y_i)$; alternatively one can regress the optimal decision on $x$ directly ($\beta^Tx$).

A positive definite kernel has PSD Gram matrices on any finite point set and generates an RKHS: the closure of finite kernel expansions with $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_jK(\bar x_i,\bar x_j)$. The kernel choice fixes the function class: linear, polynomial of degree $\le d$, or (Gaussian) a class dense in continuous bounded functions.

Regularized empirical risk minimization over an RKHS, for any loss $V$ and $\lambda\ge0$, has a minimizer that is a kernel expansion on the training points, $f(x)=\sum_ia_iK(x_i,x)$. This turns an infinite-dimensional problem into one over $a\in\mathbb R^n$.

Fit $h(z,\cdot)$ to $c(z;y_i)$ by kernel ridge regression with square loss, giving $h(z,x)=K(X,x)^T(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}c(z;Y)$, then minimize $h(z,x_0)$ over $Z$. With polynomial kernels and a norm bound $\eta$ growing with degree, the decision is asymptotically optimal as $d$ and $n$ grow.

Learn the decision rule $\hat z(x)$ in an RKHS by minimizing average realized cost plus $\lambda\|\hat z\|_H^2$; the Representer Theorem gives a finite problem in $a$ (or $a^1,\dots,a^d$). Constraints are handled by a quadratic penalty and a final projection; convex $c$ gives a convex program with $nd$ variables, and a universal kernel with $\lambda\to0$, $\lambda\sqrt n\to\infty$ gives consistency.

Newsvendor with unit cost $d$, revenue $r$, demand $y=\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\epsilon$: $\min_{z\ge0}\mathbb E[dz-r\min(z,y)|x]$. In the plots (noise 15 and 30), keropt has the lowest cost after the ex-post oracle, kerobj is at or slightly below nearest neighbors, and SAA is worst.

quiz.q: In the movie-stocking example of the L12 setup, what plays the role of $x$?
o: Number of each movie type to stock
Demand for each type of movie
quiz.e: $x$ is the observed context used to predict demand $y$. The stock levels are the decision $z$, and demand is the uncertain $y$.

quiz.q: Which kernel generates an RKHS containing only polynomials up to order $d$?
quiz.e: Polynomial kernel. The linear kernel gives only linear functions; the Gaussian kernel gives a much richer (universal) class.

quiz.q: The Representer Theorem guarantees a solution of the regularized RKHS problem of the form:
o: $f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^M\bar a_iK(\bar x_i,x)$ for arbitrary centers $\bar x_i$
quiz.e: The kernels sit on the $n$ training points only. Arbitrary centers describe a general element of $H_0$, not the solution structure.

quiz.q: In the newsvendor plots, which method has the lowest cost apart from the ex-post optimal benchmark?
quiz.e: For both noise levels keropt sits closest to the post curve. kerobj is at or slightly below nn, and SAA is clearly worst.

quiz.q: Why does the kernel prediction of the objective use square loss?
o: The conditional mean is the minimizer of expected squared error
Square loss makes $h(z,x)$ convex in the decision $z$
The Representer Theorem holds only for square loss
Square loss is robust to outliers in $c(z;y)$
quiz.e: $\mathbb E[c(z;y)|\cdot]=\arg\min_h\mathbb E[(c(z;y)-h(z,x))^2]$. The Representer Theorem holds for any loss $V$.

quiz.q: What does the kernel prediction of the optimizer (keropt) learn?
o: A function mapping $x$ directly to a decision $\hat z(x)$
A function $h(z,x)$ approximating the conditional cost
Nearest-neighbor weights over the training points
quiz.e: keropt fits $\hat z(\cdot)\in H$ by minimizing realized cost. Approximating $h(z,x)$ is kerobj.

quiz.q: Polynomial kernel with $r=1$, $d=2$: what is $K(x,x')$ for $x=(1,2)$, $x'=(3,0)$?
quiz.e: $x^Tx'=3$, so $(3+1)^2=16$. 9 forgets $r$; 10 adds $r$ after squaring; 4 forgets the power.

quiz.q: keropt's convergence theorem needs $\sup_xK(x,x)\le\kappa^2$. For the Gaussian kernel, the smallest valid $\kappa^2$ is:
quiz.e: $K(x,x)=\exp(0)=1$ for every $x$. The bandwidth $\sigma$ only matters for $x\ne x'$.

quiz.q: In the linear-regression version, $\mathbb E[c(z;y)|x_0]\approx c(z;Y)^Tw$ with $w=X(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$. What is the dimension of $w$?
quiz.e: $X$ is $n\times p$, $(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$ is $p\times1$, so $w\in\mathbb R^n$ multiplies the vector of sample costs $c(z;Y)$.

quiz.q: How does the regression-based approach differ from the Bertsimas–Kallus local approach, per the slides?
o: Predictions come from minimizing a loss, not from nearby training data
It ignores the auxiliary data $x$ entirely
It requires the cost $c$ to be linear in $y$
It replaces the weighted sum with a maximum over samples
quiz.e: Both produce weighted sums of sample costs; the regression weights come from fitting a loss function rather than proximity to $x_0$.

quiz.q: To fit the regression prediction of the optimizer $\beta^Tx$, one solves:
quiz.e: The fit minimizes realized decision cost on the data. Least squares on $y$ predicts demand, not the decision.

quiz.q: keropt with $n=200$ samples and decision $z\in\mathbb R^5$ (convex $c$, $Z=\mathbb R^5$) is a convex problem with how many variables?
quiz.e: One vector $a^t\in\mathbb R^n$ per decision coordinate: $nd=200\cdot5$. 40000 is the size of $\hat K$.

quiz.q: Constraint $f(z)=z-5\le0$ relaxed with $\psi=10$. What penalty does $z=7$ incur?
quiz.e: $\psi\max(f(z),0)^2=10\cdot2^2=40$. 20 forgets to square the violation.

quiz.q: After solving the penalized keropt problem, $\hat z(x_0)$ violates a constraint. What do the slides prescribe?
o: Use the nearest training point's decision
quiz.e: $\hat z(x_0)$ is feasible only asymptotically ($\psi\to\infty$), so a Euclidean projection onto $Z$ restores feasibility.

quiz.q: kerobj's convergence result (polynomial kernels) requires:
o: Degree $d\ge D$ and sample size $n\ge N(D)$, with $\eta$ increasing in $d$
Only $n\to\infty$ with a fixed polynomial degree
A universal kernel such as the Gaussian
quiz.e: Both degree and sample size must grow. The $\lambda$ rate and universal-kernel conditions belong to keropt's theorem.

quiz.q: Once keropt is trained, what is needed to decide for a new $x_0$ (unconstrained case)?
o: Refit $a$ with $x_0$ added to the data
quiz.e: keropt outputs a decision rule, so a new context needs only a kernel evaluation. Optimizing over $z$ for each $x_0$ is kerobj.

quiz.q: Newsvendor: $d=1$, $r=3$, order $z=10$, realized demand $y=6$. What is $c(z;y)=dz-r\min(z,y)$?
quiz.e: $10-3\cdot6=-8$ (a profit of 8). $-20$ uses $\min=z$; $-18$ forgets the purchase cost.

quiz.q: Which regularization schedule satisfies keropt's condition $\lambda\to0$ and $\lambda\sqrt n\to\infty$?
quiz.e: $n^{-1/4}\sqrt n=n^{1/4}\to\infty$. $n^{-1/2}$ gives $\lambda\sqrt n=1$, which does not diverge; the constant never goes to 0.

quiz.q: kerobj's objective can be written $h(z,x_0)=\sum_iw_ic(z;y_i)$. What is $w$?
quiz.e: $h=K(X,x_0)^T(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}c(z;Y)$ and the matrix is symmetric, so $w=(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}K(X,x_0)$. This is the Bertsimas–Kallus weighted form with regression weights.

quiz.q: Why is the keropt penalty $\lambda a^T\hat Ka$?
o: It is a ridge penalty added for numerical stability only
$\|\hat z\|_H^2=a^T\hat K^{-1}a$ by the Representer Theorem
quiz.e: It follows from the RKHS inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_jK(\bar x_i,\bar x_j)$. $\|a\|^2$ would only be right if $\hat K=I$.

quiz.q: Could $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ be the Gram matrix of a positive definite kernel at two points?
o: No: it has eigenvalue $-1$, so it is not PSD
Yes: it is symmetric with positive entries
Yes: its diagonal entries are positive
No: off-diagonal kernel entries must be zero
quiz.e: Eigenvalues are $1\pm2=3,-1$. A PD kernel needs every Gram matrix PSD; positive entries are not enough (e.g. $v=(1,-1)$ gives $v^TKv=-2$).

quiz.q: $K(\bar x_1,\bar x_1)=K(\bar x_2,\bar x_2)=1$, $K(\bar x_1,\bar x_2)=0.5$. For $f=2K(\bar x_1,\cdot)$ and $g=3K(\bar x_1,\cdot)+K(\bar x_2,\cdot)$, what is $\langle f,g\rangle_H$?
quiz.e: $2\cdot3\cdot1+2\cdot1\cdot0.5=7$. 6.5 drops the coefficient 2 on the cross term; 8 ignores the kernel values.

written.q: Compare the kernel prediction of the objective (kerobj) and of the optimizer (keropt) for $\min_{z\in Z}\mathbb E[c(z;y)|x=x_0]$: formulations, how the decision for $x_0$ is obtained, constraints, and convergence conditions.
written.m: kerobj approximates the cost surface. For each $z$, fit $h(z,\cdot)\in H$ by $\min\frac1n\sum_i(c(z;y_i)-h(z,x_i))^2+\lambda\|h(z,\cdot)\|_H^2$ (square loss because the conditional mean minimizes MSE). Closed form $h(z,x)=K(X,x)^T(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}c(z;Y)$, a weighted SAA. The decision solves $\min_{z\in Z}h(z,x_0)$, so $Z$ is handled directly. Convergence: polynomial kernels with $\|h\|\le\eta$, $\eta$ increasing in $d$, finite VC dimension, continuity, bounded sets; for $d\ge D$, $n\ge N(D)$ the cost gap exceeds $\delta$ with probability below $\epsilon$. keropt learns the policy: $\min_{\hat z\in H}\frac1n\sum_ic(\hat z(x_i);y_i)+\lambda\|\hat z\|_H^2$, which by the Representer Theorem becomes $\min_a\frac1n\sum_ic((\hat Ka)_i;y_i)+\lambda a^T\hat Ka$ (one $a^t$ per coordinate for $z\in\mathbb R^d$). The decision is $\hat z(x_0)=\sum_ia_iK(x_i,x_0)$. Constraints enter through the penalty $\psi\sum_j\max(f_j(z),0)^2$ plus a projection onto $Z$. Convex $c$ gives a convex program with $nd$ variables. Convergence holds if $c$ is Lipschitz and convex, $K$ is bounded and universal (Gaussian), $c(0;y)$ is bounded, $\lambda\to0$ and $\lambda\sqrt n\to\infty$. In the newsvendor experiment keropt had the lowest cost after the oracle.
k: kerobj fit with square loss and the closed form $K(X,x)^T(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}c(z;Y)$
keropt finite problem in $a$ from the Representer Theorem
keropt decision $\sum_ia_iK(x_i,x_0)$; penalty plus projection for constraints
Convexity with $nd$ variables when $c$ is convex
Correct convergence conditions for each (polynomial $d,n$ growth vs universal kernel and $\lambda$ rate)

written.q: Define a positive definite kernel and the RKHS it generates, state the Representer Theorem, and use them to derive the finite-dimensional keropt problem for $Z=\mathbb R$. Why is it convex when $c$ is convex in $z$?
written.m: $K$ is positive definite if every Gram matrix $[K(\bar x^i,\bar x^j)]_{i,j\le M}$ is PSD. The RKHS is the closure of $H_0=\{\sum_{i=1}^M\bar a_iK(\bar x_i,\cdot)\}$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_jK(\bar x_i,\bar x_j)$. Representer Theorem: for any loss $V$ and $\lambda\ge0$, $\min_{f\in H}\sum_iV(f(x_i);y_i)+\lambda\|f\|_H$ has a solution $f=\sum_{i=1}^na_iK(x_i,\cdot)$. For keropt take $V=c$, so $\hat z=\sum_ja_jK(x_j,\cdot)$. Then $\hat z(x_i)=\sum_ja_jK(x_j,x_i)=(\hat Ka)_i$, and by the inner product $\|\hat z\|_H^2=a^T\hat Ka$. The problem becomes $\min_{a\in\mathbb R^n}\frac1n\sum_ic((\hat Ka)_i;y_i)+\lambda a^T\hat Ka$. Convexity: $(\hat Ka)_i$ is linear in $a$, so convex $c$ composed with it is convex; $a^T\hat Ka$ is convex because $\hat K$ is PSD.
k: RKHS as the closure of kernel expansions with the stated inner product
Representer Theorem stated with kernels on the training points
Convexity argument: linear composition plus PSD quadratic

written.q: Trace the progression in L12 from local weights to kernel regression for data-driven optimization. Explain the two regression-based routes (predict the objective vs predict the optimizer) and what kernels add.
written.m: Bertsimas–Kallus: a local predictor such as kNN gives $\mathbb E[y|x_0]\approx\sum_iw(x_i,x_0)y_i$, so $\mathbb E[c(z;y)|x_0]\approx\sum_iw(x_i,x_0)c(z;y_i)$, minimized over $z$. Route 1 (predict the objective): linear regression gives $\mathbb E[c(z;y)|x_0]\approx c(z;Y)^TX(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$, again a weighted sum with $w=X(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$, but the weights come from minimizing a loss rather than from nearby data. Route 2 (predict the optimizer): assume $\arg\min_z\mathbb E[c|x]\approx\beta^Tx$, fit $\min_\beta\sum_ic(\beta^Tx_i;y_i)$ and output $\beta^Tx_0$. Both are linear in $x$. Kernels generalize them to nonlinear functions: regularized fitting over an RKHS, made finite by the Representer Theorem. This gives kerobj (weights $(\hat K+\lambda nI)^{-1}K(X,x_0)$) and keropt ($\hat z(x)=\sum_ia_iK(x_i,x)$). The Gaussian kernel's RKHS approximates any continuous bounded function.
k: Linear-regression weights $X(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$, loss-based rather than proximity-based
Kernels add nonlinearity via the RKHS and the Representer Theorem
Names the resulting kerobj and keropt forms
